clinical_knowledge.topic: Second-Degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Second-Degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes urgent hospital admission with continuous cardiac monitoring and bed rest with bathroom privileges only (high risk of unpredictable progression to complete third-degree AV block or ventricular standstill), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: frequent dizzy spells, near fainting, and heart dropping beats over 2 weeks

Key HPI features: 2-week history of recurrent, abrupt-onset dizzy spells, lightheadedness, and feeling on the verge of blacking out when walking or rising from a chair. Reports sensation of his pulse becoming exceptionally slow or dropping several beats in a row. Experienced two episodes of near-syncope where he had to grab a table to avoid falling. Denies chest pain, shortness of breath, or seizure activity. Had a pacemaker discussion years ago but never followed up.

Objective/Exam findings: Examine pulse: slow, irregular pulse at 42 bpm with intermittent dropped beats. Vitals: BP 115/68 mmHg. 12-lead ECG: normal constant PR interval on conducted beats, but sudden unexpected non-conducted P waves (dropped QRS complexes) occurring in a 2:1 or 3:2 conduction ratio with normal sinus P-P intervals (Second-Degree Atrioventricular Block - Mobitz Type II). Check QRS duration (often widened indicating infranodal His-Purkinje conduction disease). Bloods: U&Es (rule out hyperkalaemia), troponin, digoxin level if applicable.
Relevant background/PMH: hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3, osteoarthritis
Current medications: amlodipine 5mg OD, paracetamol PRN (not taking beta-blockers or rate-slowing drugs)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Second-Degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Sick sinus syndrome without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Syncope without warning — high risk of progression to complete heart block.
management_principles: Urgent hospital admission with continuous cardiac monitoring and bed rest with bathroom privileges only (high risk of unpredictable progression to complete third-degree AV block or ventricular standstill)

If severe symptomatic bradycardia or haemodynamic instability occurs: administer IV atropine (though less reliable in infranodal Mobitz II) or IV isoprenaline, and prepare transcutaneous/transvenous temporary pacing
Urgent cardiology consult for permanent dual-chamber pacemaker (PPM) implantation
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2018 ACC/AHA/HRS Guideline on the Evaluation and Management of Patients With Bradycardia and Cardiac Conduction Delay

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: frequent dizzy spells, near fainting, and heart dropping beats over 2 weeks

2-week history of recurrent, abrupt-onset dizzy spells, lightheadedness, and feeling on the verge of blacking out when walking or rising from a chair. Reports sensation of his pulse becoming exceptionally slow or dropping several beats in a row. Experienced two episodes of near-syncope where he had to grab a table to avoid falling. reference_soap.objective: Examine pulse: slow, irregular pulse at 42 bpm with intermittent dropped beats. Vitals: BP 115/68 mmHg. 12-lead ECG: normal constant PR interval on conducted beats, but sudden unexpected non-conducted P waves (dropped QRS complexes) occurring in a 2:1 or 3:2 conduction ratio with normal sinus P-P intervals (Second-Degree Atrioventricular Block - Mobitz Type II). Check QRS duration (often widened indicating infranodal His-Purkinje conduction disease). Bloods: U&Es (rule out hyperkalaemia), troponin, digoxin level if applicable.
reference_soap.assessment: Second-Degree Atrioventricular Block (Mobitz Type II) causing symptomatic bradycardia and presyncope. DDx: Mobitz Type I (Wenckebach - progressive PR prolongation before dropped beat; benign nodal disease), Complete (Third-Degree) AV Block, Sick Sinus Syndrome, drug-induced bradycardia.
reference_soap.plan: Urgent hospital admission with continuous cardiac monitoring and bed rest with bathroom privileges only (high risk of unpredictable progression to complete third-degree AV block or ventricular standstill). If severe symptomatic bradycardia or haemodynamic instability occurs: administer IV atropine (though less reliable in infranodal Mobitz II) or IV isoprenaline, and prepare transcutaneous/transvenous temporary pacing. Urgent cardiology consult for permanent dual-chamber pacemaker (PPM) implantation.

learning_objectives: Differentiate Mobitz Type II AV block (constant PR interval before suddenly dropped QRS; high risk infranodal block) from Mobitz Type I Wenckebach (progressive PR prolongation)
Recognise the high clinical danger of Mobitz Type II progressing unpredictably to complete heart block or asystole
Outline the emergency step-up bradycardia management protocol from pharmacological adjuncts to temporary and permanent pacing
Counsel elderly patients clearly regarding permanent pacemaker implantation procedure, safety, and lifestyle benefits

teaching.diagnosis: Second-Degree AV Block, Mobitz Type II
teaching.one_liner: Conduction to the ventricles fails intermittently and unpredictably. It progresses to complete block, so it needs a pacemaker.
red_flags: Syncope without warning — high risk of progression to complete heart block

must_ask.say: Do you get any warning at all, or does it come out of nowhere?
How often is this happening, and is it getting more frequent?
Are you on any heart tablets — beta blockers, digoxin, or similar?
Have you actually lost consciousness, or only come close?
Have you hurt yourself when this happened?
Have you been unusually tired or short of breath?
